articles.title: An empty CA field turned off TLS in our Kubernetes app
articles.excerpt: Our Kubernetes desktop app had a bug I'm not proud of. If you added a remote cluster with a bearer token (or a client cert, exec plugin, OIDC) and left the CA field empty, the app wrote insecure-skip-…
articles.body: Our Kubernetes desktop app had a bug I'm not proud of. If you added a remote cluster with a bearer token (or a client cert, exec plugin, OIDC) and left the CA field empty, the app wrote insecure-skip-tls-verify: true into the generated kubeconfig. No warning anywhere. So the token went to a server whose identity nobody checked. The CA field looked optional. That was the whole problem. Empty felt like "use defaults", and the default was "trust anything". Worse part: a check with the right policy already existed in the code. Nothing called it. Four forms built their kubeconfig on their own and none of them went through it.
articles.author: Rozoom News Editor

articles.title: The Test Guarding My List of Deliberate Bugs Made Every Bug Look Caught for a Month
articles.excerpt: A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory. Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this s…
articles.body: A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory. Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this setup — its first 3 chapters: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code-free-sample My agent checks its own test suite by breaking its code on purpose. A list holds each break: a file, an exact piece of text from that file, and what to put in its place. The piece is often one line, sometimes part of a line or several lines. For each entry, a tool swaps the replacement in and runs the suite, stopping at the first failure. If something fails, the break counts as caught. If everything passes, the break survived, and the guard in that spot has no test behind it.
articles.author: Sungsoo Youn

articles.title: I did my own _ — a home for people who rebuilt a famous app
articles.excerpt: A lot of good software starts with one thought: "I could build my own version of that." Somebody looks at Photoshop, or AirDrop, or Docker Desktop, and instead of only subscribing, they open a repo an…
articles.body: A lot of good software starts with one thought: "I could build my own version of that." Somebody looks at Photoshop, or AirDrop, or Docker Desktop, and instead of only subscribing, they open a repo and start building. Not a clone for the sake of a clone. Their own version. Open source, on GitHub, with a real licence. I got tired of finding those projects one at a time, so I made a place to put them together. It's called I Did My Own (idmo.app). Full disclosure up front: I run the site. The header even plays with the idea. It reads i did my own _ . The word "did" glitches into "developed" and back. Why it exists There are plenty of "alternatives to X" lists. They are useful, and they are also usually a flat pile of names.

articles.title: My templated pages were near-duplicates. A small Python check proved it, and now it runs in CI
articles.excerpt: I run a small static site of browser-based tools: image compressors, PDF converters, translators. The pages are generated by a Python script. That's convenient, until you notice Google has crawled mos…
articles.body: I run a small static site of browser-based tools: image compressors, PDF converters, translators. The pages are generated by a Python script. That's convenient, until you notice Google has crawled most of them and decided not to index them. Search Console's verdict for 38 pages was "Crawled – currently not indexed". The site is new, so part of that is just age. But when I looked at my own generator, part of it was clearly my fault: templates. How templated pages quietly become duplicates Each "compress image to N KB" page came from one function. So did each "X to Y converter" and each "language A to language B translator".

articles.title: How Do You Design a Mobile App to Work Reliably Offline?
articles.excerpt: Building a mobile app that works reliably without a connection means inverting the usual cloud architecture. Instead of treating the remote server as the target for every user action and network calls…
articles.body: Building a mobile app that works reliably without a connection means inverting the usual cloud architecture. Instead of treating the remote server as the target for every user action and network calls as a gate, the local device database becomes the single source of truth for the user interface. Network calls turn into background processes that sync changes whenever connectivity allows. With this local first approach, user actions succeed instantly with no network latency, battery drain drops, and spotty connections no longer crash or stall the app. Getting there takes discipline around data modeling, conflict resolution, sync queues, and schema lifecycle management.

articles.title: Leonid meteor shower thrills stargazers worldwide with colorful sky show (photos/video)
articles.excerpt: From colorful meteors to lingering trails, the Leonids put on a great show this year.
articles.body: The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it. The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off. Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light. The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history.

articles.excerpt: The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a constellation of Earth-observing satellites for humanitarian use, the first of which is scheduled to lift off next year.
articles.body: The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan. The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites , whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world. That plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space announced the builder of the first of those satellites : Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company. There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space.

This long-running puzzle and Easter egg hunt revolved around a cryptic mural found inside the summit cable car station, and surrounding clues at the highest point of San Andreas. The cable car station at the top of Mount Chiliad featured a cave drawing of a mountain topped by an Illuminati eye, with lines coming off the mountain connected to ancient alien-style carvings of a UFO, a cracked egg, and a jetpack. This mystery would later pay off in GTA Online, when The Doomsday Heist introduced an underground facility beneath Mount Chiliad, along with a flyable jetpack. articles.title: What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?
articles.excerpt: The Voyager 1 probe continues to fly out into interstellar space after its historic distance milestone. NASA expects it to keep working until at least 2027.
articles.body: Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft. Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 , launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s. Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035.

Original Annotated The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas Explanation: Today’s image could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue Alnitak (the Girdle): a triple star system best known for being the easternmost star in Orion’s Belt . The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse’s head at the center is the aptly named Horsehead Nebula .
